episode_thesis: Katie Kaminski argues that geopolitical risk, especially on the supply side, foreshadows inflation, which erodes bonds as a hedge and makes 60/40 vulnerable; trend, as an unbiased and opportunistic second responder, is the most robust protection across inflation regimes, with commodities as the first responder when used actively. Both speakers argue that the main cost to trend investors is behavioural: returns come from a few big months and investors lose a large share by timing, so roles, expectations, rebalancing and packaging are needed to hold it.

speakers.name: Katie Kaminski
speakers.role: Guest co-host; trend-following researcher and practitioner (co-author of a trend-following book; ETF participant)
speakers.speaker_note: Captions do not label speakers. Attributions follow the ledger corrections: the '38 of 40 years' remark and the Singapore JGB trader story are Niels's; the liquidity-as-hindrance explanation is Katie's answer to Niels's question; the dollar-weighted figure was quoted uncertainly ('about 1.7% or ... four something percent').

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following is theme-driven: it latches onto the biggest prevailing market themes, so a good trend year does not imply the year resembles earlier good years.
worldview_premises.support: Compares 2022 (energy only similar) with 2026; theme rotation in March.

worldview_premises.premise: Chaotic geopolitical and inflationary conditions are favourable for managed futures because the strategy is unbiased and reacts after the shock.
worldview_premises.support: Own years of experience; 'we like chaos'.

worldview_premises.premise: Geopolitical risk is measurable (news-based indices), is priced as a risk premium, has firm-level effects and leads inflation.
worldview_premises.support: Academic literature: Iacoviello-type index, a January paper with over 100 years of data in 44 countries.

worldview_premises.premise: Inflation is the natural predator of bonds: when inflation is the key risk, bonds co-move with stocks, their volatility rises and they lose safe-haven status.
worldview_premises.support: Her paper 'Bonds Behaving Badly'; 2022 and the last five years; 800 years of data (with Alex Greyserman).

worldview_premises.premise: 60/40 is well diversified only in a low-inflation, low-geopolitical-risk world; adding geopolitical risk and deglobalisation makes it vulnerable.
worldview_premises.support: Anchoring of her generation of investors to 60/40.

worldview_premises.premise: Bonds remain a good holding when yields are high enough to compensate; the answer to bond weakness is price, not abandoning bonds.
worldview_premises.support: Answer to a conference question 'should we have no bonds?'.

worldview_premises.premise: Familiar assets feel safer than they are, so investors are more exposed in an adverse scenario than they think.
worldview_premises.support: Investors with '2022 PTSD' from bonds.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend has no standing directional bias: it was accused of long-bond bias in the bond bull market and flips to long bonds whenever bonds trend up.
worldview_premises.support: History of the strategy; frequency argument.

worldview_premises.premise: Different inflation regimes need different protection: commodities work when inflation spikes, equities and private equity are vulnerable, and trend is the most robust across rising and falling inflation.
worldview_premises.support: AQR risk-mitigation study across rising, stable and falling inflation; sensitivity exhibit.

worldview_premises.premise: Commodities have the wanted inflation correlation but no positive carry and high volatility, so passive exposure is poor and needs active management; indices are energy-heavy.
worldview_premises.support: AQR paper discussion; commodity returns concentrated in a few big up or down years.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend returns are concentrated in a few shock months, and investors lose a large part of them by timing entry and exit.
worldview_premises.support: Quantica 'Paid for Presence': 5.6% average falls to about -0.5% without the 20 largest months; dollar-weighted returns well below index.

worldview_premises.premise: Timing and return chasing hurt in any liquid, complex strategy; patience is asymmetric across asset classes, and the ability to trade a liquid fund pulls attention to the short term.
worldview_premises.support: Contrast with private equity and real estate, which hide marks; day-trading research.

worldview_premises.premise: Institutions detach short-term emotion through formal process and change allocations mainly after governance shocks.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of institutional investors.

mechanism_chains.topic: Geopolitical risk to inflation to bond and 60/40 vulnerability

steps.from: Supply-side geopolitical risk (for example the US-Iran conflict)
steps.why: Literature shows geopolitical risk foreshadows inflation; premium is being repriced now.
Positive stock-bond correlation and higher bond volatility; bonds fail as safe haven when inflation is high and stocks fall.
The portfolio's diversification relied on a low-inflation regime.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Bonds Behaving Badly, 800-year bond data, 2022 experience, geopolitical-risk-leads-inflation paper.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Inflation stays low or yields become high enough to compensate (then bonds are attractive again); she also notes a risk-off move can restore the hedge.

steps.to: Trend reacts over weeks to months (second responder)
steps.why: Trend reallocates once the new price trend is established.

steps.to: Investors hold each piece through bad stretches
steps.why: Knowing a holding's role reduces after-the-fact reactions.

mechanism_chains.evidence: AQR risk-mitigation paper: sensitivities of 60/40, Treasuries, equities, commodities, gold, price trend and economic trend to headline, core, food and energy inflation.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Commodities fail outside inflation spikes; trend fails when a sudden risk-off reverses its equity-long, bond-short positioning.

steps.to: A few months drive the return
steps.why: Without the 20 largest months the average is slightly negative.

steps.from: Investors think they can predict the run-up
steps.to: They sell after underperformance and buy after strong runs

Rebalancing, roles, benchmarks, model portfolios, packaged products

mechanism_chains.topic: Why trend can be short bonds when discretionary managers cannot

steps.why: Follows data, so short or long is symmetric.

steps.to: Short bonds only while the trend lasts
steps.why: Drops the position when it ends, unlike a person whose job is to be short.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Bond bull market years when trend shorts did not pay; flips long when bonds rally.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: In long secular bond bull markets short positions did not pay.

decision_process.practice: Hold trend as a rules-based, direction-agnostic response to prevailing themes; do not make the call with gut feeling.
decision_process.why: Data over discretion; frequency of reaction matters.

decision_process.practice: Measure a risk before managing it: turn to the academic literature and quantitative indicators (geopolitical risk index, long-history bond data).
decision_process.why: If a quant cannot measure and analyse it, it cannot be managed.

decision_process.practice: Assign each holding a role (first responder, second responder, diversifier) against inflation and geopolitical threats, not only equity drawdowns.
decision_process.why: Roles raise the chance of holding through bad periods and avoid reacting after the fact.

decision_process.practice: Get commodity exposure through active commodity risk or trend, not passively or via energy-heavy indices.
decision_process.why: Passive commodity allocation has poor long-run risk-adjusted return and no carry.

decision_process.practice: Buy bonds when yield compensates for risk, rather than holding none.
decision_process.why: Bonds are good if the yield is high enough.

decision_process.practice: Institutions: set target portfolios, a clear role, expectations and long-term benchmarks, and rebalance (take profit into equities, add after drawdowns).
decision_process.why: Knowing 20 months generated most of the performance helps holding.

decision_process.practice: Where investors need equity-like return and diversification but cannot hold trend separately, combine equities and trend in one portable-alpha product.
decision_process.why: Packaging reduces timing behaviour; the trend piece limits losses when equities fall.

decision_process.practice: Slow down decision frequency and push the conversation to model-portfolio providers and consultants; supply them with information.
decision_process.why: More frequent decisions produce more adverse emotional decisions.

speakers.role: Host of Top Traders Unplugged; long-time trend-following industry participant
speakers.speaker_note: Host who also states views. Per ledger corrections he, not Katie, says one bad year traumatises investors despite 38 good years of 40, and tells the Singapore JGB trader story.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors and committees are anchored to past regimes and find it very hard to change; one bad year (2022) traumatises them despite decades of 60/40 working.
worldview_premises.support: Observations of investors and committees.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors apply inconsistent standards: equities or bonds can go 5 to 12 years without a new high, yet a trend fund 1 to 2 years under its high-water mark is a catastrophe; bond optimism persists after a decade of poor returns.
worldview_premises.support: Equities after 2000; a Danish pension fund that adopted leveraged risk parity near the low in rates; a European investor saying 'bonds look good again'.

worldview_premises.premise: Discretionary investors have the right narrative but under-express it (little short bond exposure in 2022; a JGB trader finds shorting highs after 25 years of buying dips hard), whereas a rules-based approach is agnostic on direction.
worldview_premises.support: Anecdotes from macro funds and a Singapore client.

worldview_premises.premise: Oil-driven higher rates, heavy Treasury issuance, AI capital demand and AI energy demand are a perfect storm that could leave traditional portfolios vulnerable for a long time.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoned from current events.

worldview_premises.premise: Protection is wanted only after the event; like insurance it must be bought beforehand, even though trend does not cost money over time.
worldview_premises.support: Insurance analogy.

worldview_premises.premise: Liquid, anonymous, daily-dealing trend products make timing worse because managers cannot coach investors through drawdowns.
worldview_premises.support: Own experience of ETF and mutual-fund investors being anonymous.

worldview_premises.premise: Commodity scarcity narratives fuel late commodity adds, and commodity ETFs can perform poorly because of roll yield and construction.
worldview_premises.support: Ukraine-era aluminium story that did not materialise.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Dollar-weighted investor return figure was quoted uncertainly ('1.7%' or 'four something percent'), so the size of the timing penalty is not established.
The claim that geopolitical risk leads inflation rests on one January paper; no horizon or effect size given.
Niels believes most trend peers are short bonds, but this is unsupported by data in the episode.

Katie's reason why a risk-off move is dangerous (long equities, short bonds positioning) is not stated; it is a reader inference. Also the list of good commodity years (2014, 2022, 2026) is garbled in conversation about long and short sides.
Claim that 2026 is a hedged year (AI equities and inflation bonds offsetting) is qualitative; no attribution numbers given. The 'chaos is good for trend' view is not tied to a measurable proxy.
The trend barometer reading of 50 is read as 'strong' without definition of the scale.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Geopolitical risk index levels (including the Bloomberg-listed measure), headline vs core/food/energy inflation, stock-bond correlation and bond volatility, bond yields relative to inflation compensation, fall catalysts named by Katie (US elections, AI concern, risk-off), trend barometer. Horizons are months to a year; Katie sees inflation risk premium repricing as ongoing.
reader_inferences: (reader) The responder framework implies positioning should be judged by the type of inflation threat, so a commodity sleeve and trend sleeve are not substitutes.
(reader) Katie and Niels both frame trend as a hold-and-wait strategy, so their forecasts are regime descriptions rather than price targets.
(reader) The episode contains no explicit sizing rule, only roles and rebalancing between trend and equities.
